The story concludes with a prayer, asking Jesus for forgiveness and salvation through faith, underscoring the urgency and eternal significance of that decision.

Title: Room 310
Subject: Basic Gospel
Author: Chick
Responses:
Danny O’Hara hated hospitals—they gave him the creeps. One day, as Danny and his friend Charlie arrived at the hospital, Charlie asked which room Danny was in. They were told it was room 310, and they agreed to check it out.

As they headed toward the room, Charlie warned Danny not to mention cancer to Danny because Danny already knew he was seriously ill. Despite knowing the grim reality, they tried to act as if nothing was wrong as they reached room 310.

Inside, some men talked about how unfortunate it would be to die this way, while trying to stay positive. They greeted Danny warmly, bringing cigars as a gesture of support. They encouraged him and expressed their belief that everyone was pulling for him, but Danny humorously said the doctor told him he'd be staying for a while. 

Charlie teased Danny about his charm with the nurses, and although Danny joked back, the mood soon turned serious when Charlie asked about Danny's uncle John. Danny unintentionally revealed that Uncle John had died of cancer, but Charlie advised him never to mention that in front of Danny.

The men said their goodbyes, promising to come back and keep their fingers crossed for Danny’s recovery. After they left, a chaplain named Collins tried to talk to Danny, but Danny angrily rejected him, saying he'd rather be with his friends than anyone with "religious stuffed shirts."

Danny's anger grew as he dismissed the chaplain's offer, insisting he was going where all his friends were going—implying hell—and that he'd have a good time there. When the chaplain spoke about the dangers of hell, Danny cursed at him and demanded he leave.

A week later, Danny was struggling with his faith and the absence of his friends, who hadn't returned to visit. He was convinced that they were too busy and was defensive when the chaplain tried to reach out again, rejecting his attempts to talk about faith.

Danny’s condition worsened, and the hospital informed that his situation was becoming critical. Despite medication being increased to alleviate pain, Danny wished he were already asleep forever.

One day, a nurse tried to engage Danny about love, though Danny interpreted it as sex, joking that those days were over. The nurse then offered to tell him a story, which reluctantly Danny accepted.

The nurse told a story about two Chinese brothers in early 1900s San Francisco. The elder brother deeply loved his younger brother. One day, the younger brother caused a fatal fight, ran home with bloodied clothes, and the elder brother tried to protect him by taking the blame and was executed, while the younger brother confessed but was spared.

Danny acknowledged it was a touching story but doubted anyone would ever do such a thing for him. Danny’s expression changed when the chaplain reminded him that when Jesus went to the cross, He did it for him to wash away his sins, showing how much God loved him.

The chaplain asked Danny if he would receive Jesus as his Lord. Danny was frustrated and in pain, yelling for the nurse to give him medication. As it was administered, the chaplain gently reminded Danny of the hope that lay ahead.

The chaplain told Danny that he could miss out on getting a new, perfect body free from pain and full of joy. Danny was puzzled, but the chaplain explained that Jesus would return with great power and that Danny could be part of that eternal kingdom.

The chaplain urged Danny not to forsake those who didn’t visit him anymore and told him about God's love and plans for him. Danny confessed concern over his past sins and wondered if God could forgive him.

The chaplain assured him that God already knew everything and was ready to forgive if Danny confessed. Danny decided to open his heart, asking Jesus for salvation and help.

Later, the chaplain asked if Danny had truly committed his heart to Jesus, and Danny said yes. Danny expressed newfound peace and genuine understanding of God's love. Charlie asked Danny a playful question about who loved Jesus more, and although Danny replied that Jesus loved him most, they both agreed that love was wonderful.

Feeling relieved and grateful, Danny reflected on how glad he was to be on this path rather than dying of a heart attack. He expressed gratitude for understanding God's love, looking forward to eternity filled with God’s love, thankful he made it through.

The story closes with a reminder from scripture about God's love and the invitation for everyone to receive Jesus as their Lord and Savior.

Title: Rotten Rodney
Subject: Basic Gospel
Author: Chick
Responses:
A man named Rotten Rodney was seen walking confidently, whistling, with a cane. A masked figure watching him through binoculars thought Rodney was a stuck-up big shot, assuming his pockets were bulging with money. Suddenly, the masked man pulled out a gun and demanded Rodney's money, insisting it rightfully belonged to him. When Rodney refused, the man shot him, saying it was for looking down on people like him. Rodney collapsed as the man lamented about never being shown any respect.

Police arrived at the scene, with a cat casually observing. One officer declared that the videotape would reveal the killer's identity. Watching the tape, the officers identified the culprit as Rotten Rodney, who had attempted to frame someone else. They called for a SWAT team to arrest Rodney, cautioning that he was armed and dangerous.

Rodney was found inside a house, furious that the police invaded his home and concerned about his civil rights. Taken to city jail, Rodney protested that the man on the tape wasn't him, claiming he looked just a little like him but was better looking. The detective dismissed his lies. At the trial, despite Rodney's insistence that he was innocent and framed, he was found guilty. The judge sentenced him to life imprisonment, acknowledging it as cruel and unusual punishment. Rodney accused everyone of destroying an innocent man.

Six years later, Rodney was told he was getting a new cellmate, but he didn't want one and was told to accept what he was given. Rodney's new cellmate asked if he snored, warning him that he would soon find out. The cellmate introduced himself as Little Jackie Jones, who claimed innocence despite being lifer as well. Jackie previously spent three months in solitary confinement because other inmates didn't like him.

Jackie eventually revealed that he was in prison because he had strangled two of his former cellmates for snoring. Rodney was disturbed by the revelation and felt terrible, telling the prison chaplain he hadn't slept and hated him. Rodney confessed he didn't believe in God and resented the chaplain's laughter.

The chaplain visited Rodney with small books about faith, which terrified Rodney. He was skeptical but talked to the chaplain about Jesus. The chaplain explained that Jesus is God Almighty who died for people's sins, and that God promised to wipe away every terrible sin if one truly repents and believes. The chaplain encouraged Rodney to admit he was a sinner, ask Jesus for forgiveness, and live for Him.

Rodney prayed on his knees and accepted Jesus as his Savior, experiencing forgiveness and peace. The next morning, Rodney appeared healthier and told Jackie he was saved, surprising them both since Rodney snored but was still alive. However, rumors of a deadly prison riot began to spread.

Six days later, Jackie was warned not to preach in the yard, but he insisted it was his duty. Suddenly, a riot broke out, led by a faction aiming to kill guards and other inmates. The violence lasted over six hours, leaving 79 dead and 261 hospitalized. Both Rodney and Jackie were stabbed to death during the chaos.

After their deaths, angels took their souls to stand before God. Jackie was welcomed to the joy of the Lord, praised for having no sins on his soul, and entered heaven to be with God forever. In contrast, Rodney was condemned for rejecting God, cursed and sentenced to eternal fire prepared for the devil. His soul was doomed to burn forever.

The story ends with a message urging readers to ask Jesus for forgiveness before judgment comes, offering a salvation decision form to declare faith in Jesus and receive eternal life.

Title: Royal Affair, The
Subject: Bible Stories
Author: Carter & 3rd
Responses:
Here is the comic's story in written form:

A woman revealed she had a secret video proving that a senator had sexually harassed her. When the senator's attorney asked if she had lied, the woman indignantly defended her integrity. But when the prosecutor played the videotape in court, her accusation was confirmed. The senator pleaded for understanding but was called a rat by the woman, who sued him for divorce.

The story then shifts to a biblical account. It reflects on the time when Israel was terrorized by the giant Goliath, leaving the armies paralyzed by fear. God raised up David, a young shepherd, to slay this evil monster. David became a hero, and later God made him king, promising that Christ would come through his lineage.

God always exposes sin, and the story recounts how David committed a grievous sin. One night, instead of leading his armies to battle, David stayed at home, which was the worst decision of his life. That night, David's close walk with God ended abruptly when he saw Bathsheba, the most beautiful woman he had ever seen. Satan filled his mind with lust.

David ordered Bathsheba brought to his chambers, even though she was the wife of Uriah. David thought they were alone, but the universe was recording everything. That night, David broke three of God's Ten Commandments: he coveted Bathsheba, he stole her, and he committed adultery by having sex with her.

Two weeks later, Bathsheba was pregnant, which ruined David's life and hardened his heart against God. To cover his sin, David plotted to have Uriah go home to sleep with his wife, but Uriah stayed at the king's door. David then tried to get Uriah drunk, but when that failed, he resorted to cold-blooded murder by sending Uriah to the hottest part of the battle where he was left to die.

David married Bathsheba before the baby was born, thinking he had gotten away with it, but God sent the prophet Nathan to expose the scandal. Nathan told David a story of a rich man who butchered a poor man's beloved lamb instead of taking from his own flock.

David, not realizing the story was about him, said the man deserved to die for his cruelty. Nathan then revealed the truth, saying, "THOU art the man!" He told David that although God made him king, because he murdered Uriah and stole his wife, the sword would never leave his house.

David was deeply cut to the heart and confessed his sin to God. God forgave him, but Nathan warned that the child born would surely die. After seven days, the baby died and went to heaven. The comic reassures readers that all babies who die go to heaven, which comforted David amid his tremendous loss.

David's family endured immense suffering because of his sin, including murder, rape, and incest. The story emphasizes that God has always hated adultery, and in the Old Testament, the penalty was death. Today, many families are destroyed by adultery, which God still hates.

After death, every act of adultery will be revealed, and no one will be able to hide from God's judgment. But God, in His love, made a way for adulterers and adulteresses to be forgiven through Jesus Christ.

Jesus died on the cross for our sins, rose from the dead, and promises eternal life to anyone who believes in Him. He said He is preparing a place in Heaven for believers. If you confess your sins and accept Jesus as your Lord and Savior, His blood will wash away all sin.

The story ends with a warning that playing around with someone else's spouse brings devastating consequences, including exposing your family to diseases, curses, and God's fiery judgment. The best choice is to repent and follow God's path, just as David eventually did.

Title: Sacrifice, The
Subject: Bible Stories
Author: Carter
Responses:
The story begins with Abraham and Sarah feeling incredulous about God's promise that they would have a son named Isaac. Both felt they were too old—Abraham was 76 years old, and Sarah believed her body had long dried up. Doubting the promise, Sarah proposed a plan: her Egyptian servant, Hagar, could bear a child for them. Abraham agreed, and Hagar conceived, bringing joy to Sarah initially.

However, tensions soon rose. Hagar became proud and looked down on Sarah, causing deep anger and conflict between the two women. Sarah blamed Abraham for the situation, saying that now Hagar despised her. Abraham was caught between them but allowed Sarah to decide what to do with Hagar. Sarah declared she would throw Hagar out, and Hagar fled, feeling rejected.

An angel found Hagar by a fountain in the wilderness, naming her unborn child Ishmael and promising that he would become a great nation. The angel instructed Hagar to return and submit to Sarah.

Abraham loved Ishmael and hoped he would be his heir. Still, God made it clear that Christ's lineage would come through Isaac, not Ishmael. Isaac was born when Sarah was 90, fulfilling God's promise and bringing Abraham great joy.

Yet, troubles in the camp emerged: Ishmael, at 14, was jealous and made fun of Isaac, which endangered Isaac. Sarah demanded Abraham send Hagar and Ishmael away. Though broken-hearted, Abraham complied, acting under God's will. Hagar and Ishmael wandered in the wilderness, suffering from thirst and despair, but an angel told Hagar to lift up Ishmael, promising he would become a great nation. God provided a well of water, saving Ishmael's life. Ishmael grew up in the wilderness, married an Egyptian woman, and became the father of the Arab nations.

Later, God tested Abraham by instructing him to take Isaac to the land of Moriah and offer him as a burnt offering. Though shocked, Abraham prepared for the journey, taking Isaac, two young men, and wood for the sacrifice. After three days, they reached the place of sacrifice, and Abraham built an altar, placed the wood on it, and laid Isaac upon the altar. Trusting God, Abraham stretched out his hand to slay his son.

At that moment, an angel stopped him, declaring not to harm Isaac. Abraham's faith and love for God were proven greater than his love for his son. Abraham then saw a ram caught by its horns in a thicket and offered it as a burnt offering in Isaac's place. Isaac was saved.

Isaac became the father of Jacob, leading to the nation of Israel. Many years later, a divine miracle brought the birth of Jesus Christ, God's Son, who came from heaven. Jesus became the final sacrifice for the whole world, fulfilling God’s promise that through Isaac’s line all nations would be blessed.

Jesus demonstrated that He is the way, the truth, and the life, and only through Him can people come to the Father. He shed His precious blood to cleanse humanity's sins and victoriously rose from the dead three days later. Jesus will return in power and glory, and the story concludes with a call for readiness for His return.

Title: Satan Comes To Salem
Subject: Salem Witch Trials
Author: Chick
Responses:
The story begins with a discussion about Salem, famously known for the witch trials. Contrary to the popular belief that Salem was a place where witches were killed, it was actually the beginning of religious intolerance against civil rights, disguised as fighting witches.

In the 1690s, while Europe was terrified by the Roman Catholic Inquisition, Satan made a brief two-year visit to America with the aim of destroying the Puritans. During this time, a group of young, bored, church-going girls terrorized an entire community, holding the lives of the townspeople in their hands. These girls were responsible for twenty deaths, and people were afraid even to look at them.

Life in Salem Village was harsh; bitter family feuds, freezing winters, Indian raids, and land disputes created an atmosphere of misery and hate. The village had no pastor, and the church was empty and directionless. Satan found this environment perfect for his intentions.

Thomas Putnam, a key figure in the village with many enemies, despised by his wife Ann, hired Samuel Parris as the new pastor. Parris, educated at Harvard but disliked for his arrogance and demand for unusual and expensive terms, was unpopular. When conflict erupted, he was in the middle of it, backed by Putnam’s crowd. Many who opposed him were eventually hanged.

The girls, led by Abigail Williams, began communicating with spirits and learned to look tortured by witches. Their fascination with spirits and fortune-telling grew until things spiraled out of control. One night, Abigail screamed that she was being bitten, gaining attention. Other girls joined her, pretending to be victims of witchcraft, which worked to their advantage.

To justify executing witches, the villagers misused the Old Testament, condemning witches to death but ignoring New Testament teachings of forgiveness and love. The “Reverend” Samuel Parris, the accusers, and the magistrates pronounced condemnation on many souls as they were sent to their deaths.

To be saved, belief in Jesus Christ was necessary. Jesus, Almighty God and Creator, had come to the world to save humanity from sin by his death and resurrection.

Meanwhile, back in Salem, Ann Putnam joined the girls as an accuser, targeting those with whom her family had disputes. Innocent people were accused, including Sarah Good, a homeless woman, and Little Dorsey, Good’s four-year-old daughter, who was accused of witchcraft after her mother was hanged.

Giles Cory refused to confess to witchcraft and was tortured to death. God-fearing grandmothers were taken from their homes and imprisoned. Pretty women were forced to undress and be examined for devil’s marks, enduring total humiliation.

Parris forced his slave Tituba to confess to witchcraft under duress, which energized the accusers and crowds who hung onto every accusation. The accused were executed based on "spectral evidence" that seemed unverifiable, but many were still hanged.

The trials spread as other villages called on the girls to identify witches, filling jails with suspects. Eventually, the girls invented special evidence against Mary Phips, the governor's wife’s relative. The trials were stopped only when this was tried, ending the witch hunt in the U.S. Salem was devastated, and the Puritan reputation was permanently tarnished.

Satan returned to supervise the Roman Catholic Inquisition in Europe, which continued killing for centuries, producing millions of victims.

Today, witches use the story for Halloween attention, but many forget about the coming judgment where every action and thought will be exposed before Jesus Christ. Those who believe in Him and accept Him as Savior will be saved, while those who reject Him will face eternal judgment.

The story ends with a call to take the gospel seriously, emphasizing salvation through Jesus Christ and the consequences of rejecting Him, quoting scripture to support the message. It warns of an eternal judgment where everyone will give an account of their lives before God.

Title: Scam, The
Subject: Bible Stories
Author: Chick
Responses:
Frank was approached by a seemingly desperate old couple trying to sell their car. They insisted Frank would love it, saying they had only driven it for four months. The man smelled a bit off, but the couple begged Frank to help them with just $500, claiming the doctor would sue them if they didn't make the final payment that day.

Touched by their story, Frank gave them the money. Yet, when Frank asked how he would get to the hospital, they said they couldn't drive him and that they were waiting for their lawyer at the coffee shop. They told Frank to take the car, pay the doctor, and drop it off, thanking him as they left. Frank was left feeling foolish, realizing he'd been conned.

Six hours later, at the police station, Frank tearfully recounted how he was scammed. The officers showed him photos of wanted criminals, "Slick Willy" and "Mean Molly," who were known con artists in five states. Frank was overwhelmed by his own gullibility.

Later, Bob, a compassionate man, approached Frank and offered to buy him dinner, having heard about Frank's ordeal. During their meal, Bob started talking about a Biblical figure named Joshua, explaining that Joshua was Moses' right-hand man and a general chosen by God to lead the Israelites into the Promised Land.

Bob described how the Israelites had spent 40 years in the desert and how God commanded Joshua to destroy the wicked inhabitants of the land, to make no deals with them whatsoever. However, Joshua was conned by the Gibeonites, a group who deceived him into making a treaty with them by pretending to come from a far country and offering old, moldy provisions.

The princes of Israel were fooled, and Joshua agreed to let the Gibeonites live, a mistake he only realized three days later. This led to war declared against the Gibeonites by other kings who were angry about the treaty.

Bob explained that Satan was behind both the Gibeonites’ and the old couple's scams, calling Satan the "daddy of all con men." He stressed that the issue wasn't what the con artists did but that their sins were unforgiven, and nothing unclean could enter heaven.

Frank, thinking he might be an angel and not in trouble, was surprised when Bob told him he was at risk of eternal damnation unless he gave his heart to Christ. Bob asked if Frank had heard the Gospel before, but Frank admitted he had not really listened.

Bob explained how all people have sinned and how God sent His Son, Jesus Christ, to save humanity from hell. Jesus was beaten, suffered, died on the cross, and then rose three days later. Believing in Him and putting trust in Him leads to forgiveness and entry into heaven.

There is no other way to heaven than through Jesus, as He said, "I am the way, the truth, and the life." Frank wanted to pray, and Bob guided him to ask Jesus to save him and receive Him as Lord and Savior.

Fifteen minutes later, the police returned with good news—they had caught the criminals and recovered Frank’s $500. Frank exclaimed this was the greatest day of his life.

Bob warned Frank not to let Satan con him out of eternal life and encouraged him to commit fully to Jesus, reminding him of the Scripture Psalm 50:15, which promises deliverance to those who call on God in times of trouble.

Thus, Frank learned both a worldly lesson about cons and a spiritual lesson about the greatest salvation offered through Jesus Christ.

Title: Scar, The
Subject: Basic Gospel
Responses:
This is the story of a girl named Minya in Bita Genet, Keffa Zone, Ethiopia, on June 2nd, 2005. Ali spotted her and suddenly grabbed her from behind, catching her by surprise. Minya struggled, shouting for help, but Ali was determined. He pushed her into a van and drove off fast, slamming the doors behind them as Minya screamed for release.

Inside the van, Ali declared in a forceful voice that Minya would be his wife by Allah’s command. Minya immediately refused, but Ali threatened to convince her the hard way, striking her with a stick. Minya’s screams filled the air with despair.

Meanwhile, some bystanders noticed the van and recognized Minya. A young boy shouted, “Hey, that’s Minya!” and ran to tell his parents. Her family quickly decided to call the police to find her.

The police arrived at a nearby hut and advised Minya’s family to hide until nightfall for safety. Minya, feeling lost and scared, prayed silently, asking God why this was happening to her and feeling abandoned.

Back with her captors, Ali gave Minya an ultimatum: marry him within a week or never see her parents again. Ali reassured her father, Kemal, that the police would return, and they planned to move to safety when night came.

The police spoke with Minya’s family, saying they had an idea of which clan had taken her. Sergeant Wedajo promised the family that his officers would watch the roads closely and that they would all pray for God's guidance.

On the seventh day, Ali confronted Minya one last time, asking if she would marry him. When she refused, he became enraged, threatening her with a beating she wouldn’t forget. Desperate, Minya cried out to Jesus for help.

Suddenly, from the darkness, a roaring sound filled the air. Lions appeared, frightening Ali and his men. The lions attacked Ali, leaving him wounded, while the kidnappers struggled to fend them off.

In the chaos, Ali’s men argued about what to do with Minya, some suggesting the lions should have her, while others pushed to start the van and escape. They banged and shoved, trying to get out of the dangerous situation.

Minya sat quietly near the lions, thanking God for their protection. The next morning, the police arrived. Recognizing her, they quietly called out, “There she is! Psst! Minya!” Minya joyfully reunited with her parents, and that day marked a significant change in her life.

The extraordinary event of lions saving Minya sparked change in Ethiopia; the practice of forced-marriage kidnapping began to be outlawed. Ali and Ahmed, two men discussing the event years later, reflected on how Minya had been trapped without hope and likened themselves to her in some ways.

They talked about sin, acknowledging that everyone disobeys God and faces judgment, a trap that leads to death. They recognized they were powerless to fix their brokenness on their own and felt doomed.

But then they discussed how God sent a Lion to help humanity—the Lion of the tribe of Judah, who is Jesus Christ. This Lion came to save people by forgiving their sins. Though Jesus was without sin, He was hated and killed by His own people. Jesus paid the price for sin by dying on the cross but rose again three days later, bringing hope to everyone who believes in Him and trusts Him.

Mikael confessed to Ahmed that he had been a rebel too long and longed to be forgiven. Ahmed eagerly helped him, and moments later, Mikael prayed with all his heart, asking Jesus for forgiveness and guidance. He felt like a new person, as if a great weight had been lifted, all because of those lions—just like the ones that saved Minya.

Curious, Ahmed asked what happened to the lions, but no one knew; such a thing hadn’t happened since.

Mikael explained that he hadn’t told everything yet, revealing scars on his side from that day. Twenty years ago, he was known as Ali, the man who kidnapped Minya. But through faith in Jesus Christ, both Ali and Ahmed were saved.

The story ended with an invitation for others to believe on the Lord Jesus Christ to be saved, admitting one’s sin, accepting Jesus’ sacrifice, and welcoming Him into one’s heart—a chance for lasting change and hope.

Title: Scoundrel, The
Subject: Bible Stories
Author: Carter
Responses:
Two nations were growing inside Rebekah. She was in great pain and cried out to Isaac, saying, "Isaac, the pain is killing me!" Isaac replied, "Pray about it." The Lord explained to Rebekah that she was carrying twins who would change the course of history.

When Rebekah gave birth, the firstborn, Esau, was red and hairy, while the second, Jacob, was smooth-skinned. Despite being little children, these two would become responsible for significant world events.

Esau became a cunning hunter and was Isaac’s favorite. However, Rebekah loved Jacob, who had his own special skills and was sneaky like his mother.

One day, Isaac told Esau, "My son, someday all this will be yours." Since Esau was the firstborn, the birthright belonged to him by law. But greedy Jacob had other ideas. He thought, "If the birthright was mine, I would have power, property, and respect." He said, "Ahhh, I've got an idea."

Later, starving Esau entered Jacob’s tent and begged for food, saying, "Feed me, Jacob! I'm starving." Jacob saw his chance. He offered his stew in exchange for Esau’s birthright and asked, "Is it a deal?" Esau agreed, saying, "It's a deal. I swear! It's no good to me if I die." Jacob thought, "The fool! Now the birthright is mine... at last!"

Esau despised his birthright, and that is why God hated him, but tricky Jacob still needed his father's blessing to make the birthright official.

Old Isaac, who was blind and near death, called Esau and asked him to kill a deer and prepare his favorite dish so Isaac could bless him. Jacob’s evil plan was now in danger.

Rebekah overheard the conversation and knew how important the blessing was. She knew God first gave it to Isaac’s father, Abraham, who said, "I will bless them that bless thee, and curse him that curseth thee." So, Rebekah devised a plan to get Jacob the blessing. She made a stew and disguised Jacob as Esau by putting a goat skin on his neck and hands so Isaac would feel him and think he was Esau.

Jacob expressed concern, "But I'm smooth-skinned. If Father realizes it’s me, he will curse me." Rebekah replied, "Then that curse be upon me! Do as I say! Bring me two young goats... and hurry!"

Esau knew how important the blessing was, so he quickly killed a deer and headed home. The question was: who would get to Isaac first?

Jacob entered Isaac's tent and lied through his teeth. Isaac asked, "Who are you, my son?" Jacob responded, "I'm Esau." Isaac said, "Come close, so I can feel you." Isaac noticed the voice was Jacob’s but the hands were Esau’s and wondered how he could kill the deer so quickly. Jacob answered confidently, "Because the Lord thy God brought it to me." Isaac accepted it, bought it, and gave the blessing to Jacob, the scoundrel.

Isaac declared to Jacob, "Let people serve thee, and nations bow down to thee: be lord over thy brethren..." Thus, Jacob received the blessing, much to Esau’s shock.

Esau was furious. He shouted, "Father! How COULD you?" and threatened, "I’ll kill him!" despite his father's explanation that the blessing was given to Jacob.

Realizing Esau’s anger, Rebekah instructed Jacob to flee to her brother Laban in Haran and stay there until Esau calmed down.

In Haran, Jacob fell in love with a beautiful girl named Rachel, who was the daughter of his uncle Laban. Though Jacob was a scoundrel, he was no match for Laban’s shrewdness.

Jacob wanted Rachel for his wife, so he agreed to work for Laban seven years in exchange for her hand. Jacob loved Rachel so much that the hard labor flew by.

Finally, the wedding day came. Jacob was thrilled to be marrying Rachel, but the next morning he discovered Laban had tricked him by giving him Leah, Rachel’s older sister. Laban explained it was their custom for the eldest daughter to marry first, and Jacob would have to work another seven years for Rachel.

Years later, Jacob left Haran with his wives and wealth. People wondered how he became so rich, but he started off broke and left wealthy.

Now Jacob had a new problem: he feared his brother Esau’s anger. He prayed to the Lord, pleading for protection for himself and his family.

The dreaded meeting with Esau turned out to be a time of great rejoicing. However, their offspring became deadly enemies, with Esau’s descendants becoming the Arabs of today.

God changed Jacob’s name to Israel, and his sons became the twelve tribes of Israel. Jesus Christ came from one of those sons, Judah.

Only one son, Joseph, was kind and Christ-like; he was Israel’s favorite. Although Joseph’s brothers hated him and were scoundrels like their father, God loved them and blessed them in spite of themselves.

Though everyone was a sinner, God loves us all. Jesus said that evil comes from the heart and that all have sinned. But God sent Jesus into the world not to condemn it but to save it.

Because of sin, we are lost and headed for hell. But Isaiah said our sins, though red like scarlet, will be made white as snow. Without the shedding of blood, there is no forgiveness. Jesus, God’s Son, shed His blood to wash away our sins. He died, was buried, and rose again three days later, and now He is in heaven.

God offers everyone a special gift—eternal life through Jesus Christ. Those who accept must not be scoundrels in rejecting the gift and spending eternity separated from God.

Jesus promised to prepare a place in heaven for all who love Him and said, "In my Father’s house are many mansions."

This is the story of Jacob and Esau, showing how human failings and God’s grace intertwine in history, and how through Jesus Christ, redemption is possible for all.

Title: Scream
Subject: Hell
Author: Chick
Responses:
Two men, Charlie and Sonny, arrive at a shabby warehouse. Sonny asks Charlie if this is the right place. Charlie instructs Sonny to grab some gasoline and follow him. As Charlie drinks whiskey, Sonny asks how much the owner is paying Charlie to burn down the building. Charlie reveals he’s getting $1,000 now and another $1,000 once the place is completely destroyed.

Charlie pours gasoline and lights the building on fire. Sonny tells Charlie that he's leaving, but Charlie urges Sonny to keep moving as the fire spreads. Suddenly, Charlie trips, falls into some gasoline, and catches fire.

Inside the blaze, Charlie screams in agony as he burns. Firefighters respond to the scene, quickly locating the warehouse at Vine and Maple. Crowds watch as firemen work to contain the inferno. One firefighter fears Charlie must be dead, but another wonders if it was arson.

Amidst the chaos, firefighters warn each other that the roof is going to collapse. Fred, a firefighter, rushes up the stairs after detecting a possible survivor. He crashes through the ceiling but is still alive. Fellow firefighters find Fred and try to save him from the growing blaze.

Fred is rushed to the hospital, taken to the burn ward where his condition is critical. Two weeks later, the arsonist—Charlie—is found dead in the burnt warehouse, on the first floor.

The following week at the hospital, Fred’s visitor, Bob Williams, is introduced to Fred’s wife. They have been praying for Fred's recovery. Fred tells Bob he keeps having nightmares and flashbacks about the fire—the smoke and flames were like hell itself.

Bob tells Fred that though he’s not an expert on hell, Jesus is. Fred asks for clarification, and Bob explains that Jesus, whom the Bible identifies as God, described hell in very real terms. He quotes the Bible, saying Jesus gave warnings about hell, which Fred thought was just a swear word.

Bob shares a story Jesus told about a rich man and a beggar named Lazarus. The wealthy man lived in luxury, while Lazarus suffered near his gate. When they died, Lazarus was taken by angels to Abraham’s side, but the rich man ended up in torment in hell.

The rich man begs Abraham to send Lazarus to relieve his suffering with water, but Abraham reminds him of the choices made in life and the consequences. Bob explains that hell is a real place of eternal torment, where people remember everything and endure pain, thirst, and regret.

Fred listens as Bob tells him about a great gulf between heaven and hell, which no one can cross. The rich man even pleaded for Lazarus to warn his family, but Abraham said that people wouldn’t listen even with such warnings.

Bob goes on to tell Fred that hell is a furnace of fire that never goes out, filled with people weeping and gnashing their teeth in pain because all hope is gone. When Fred asks if anyone ever escapes hell, Bob says no—there is no second chance after death without God’s forgiveness.

Bob describes Judgment Day, when Jesus will sit on His throne and judge the billions who died in sin. Those who didn’t believe God’s word will be sent to the Lake of Fire for eternity.

Fred hears that Jesus knew people like him were guilty and totally lost, so He sacrificed Himself on the cross to wash away their sins. Jesus was tortured, died, buried, and rose again three days later—a gift of love from God.

Bob explains that God offers this gift so people can be forgiven and go straight to heaven. Fred wants that gift but fears being judged by Jesus. Bob tells him the only way to avoid judgment is to turn to Jesus, accept His sacrifice, and ask for forgiveness.

Fred prays, asking Jesus to save him, forgive his sins, and be his Savior. Bob tells Fred he is now a new creature in Christ.

Bob reminds Fred that being forgiven is the most important thing in life, warning that everyone will be judged someday based on their thoughts, words, and actions.

The story ends with a reminder that the choice between heaven and hell is up to each individual, and there is no excuse to avoid deciding. Heaven or hell—the choice is yours.

Title: Secret of Prayer
Subject: For Christians
Author: Chick
Responses:
The story begins with Elijah, a prophet who prayed down fire from heaven, as recorded in 1 Kings 18:38. His prayers held back rain for three years because of Israel’s wickedness, according to James 5:17. Later, Elijah prayed for rain to come, refreshing the land as stated in James 5:18. The power of fervent prayer by a righteous man is affirmed in James 5:16.

Daniel, a man who dared to pray despite danger, was thrown into a den of lions but was saved because God heard his prayers. Daniel served under three rulers—Nebuchadnezzar, Belshazzar, and Darius—and took time to pray three times daily despite his responsibilities.

Moving into the New Testament, Jesus Christ prayed to His Father in heaven. Jesus would rise early before daybreak to pray, demonstrating that He is the master of prayer (Mark 1:35). When asked by His disciples to teach them to pray, Jesus gave them a model prayer (Matthew 6:9–13), emphasizing that they should not pray with vain repetitions (Matthew 6:7). The pattern Jesus taught includes exalting the Father, praying for His kingdom to come, asking for daily necessities, forgiving others, seeking protection from temptation, giving glory to God, praising Him, and ending the prayer in Jesus' name (with specific scriptural references for each point).

Jesus also taught that prayer should be private and sincere, not for public show, instructing believers to pray in secret where God rewards openly (Matthew 6:6). Believers are encouraged to have daily private prayer time with their Father because God is waiting to speak with them.

Even when feeling cold or prayerless, believers should enter the presence of God, focusing on His willingness to give rather than what they can offer. Scripture assures that God already knows our needs before we ask (Matthew 6:8).

The story of George Müller illustrates how faith in prayer works: he once prayed for three sacks of flour, and the request was answered by an unexpected visitor bringing exactly what was needed that night.

On the day of Pentecost, the Holy Spirit came to dwell in believers (Acts 2:2–3), transforming them. When a person accepts Jesus as their Savior, they are born again, their sins forgiven, and their body becomes a temple of the Holy Spirit (1 Corinthians 6:19, 2 Timothy 1:14).

However, new Christians often face spiritual attacks on their prayer life, such as distractions of obscenity or profanity. When this happens, they should plead the blood of Jesus and command Satan to leave in Jesus' name. Some become bored or fall asleep during prayers, questioning why God should listen to them.

Reading about great prayer warriors like David Brainerd can inspire believers, though it may make them feel inadequate. The secret is to pray in the Spirit and truth, mentally putting oneself to death to sin and alive in Christ (Romans 6:11, Jude 1:20). Christians must acknowledge that they cannot worship God perfectly on their own but rely on the Holy Spirit to pray through them (Romans 8:26-27).

The prayers of faithful people in the past, such as David Livingstone, David Brainerd, C.T. Studd, and Hudson Taylor, have helped raise spiritual giants who labored among unreached people groups. For example, in India, over 50,000 villages have never heard the name of Jesus, spurring believers to pray fervently for harvest laborers to spread the gospel. Mission leaders have shared poignant stories of prayer needs for unreached areas like Nepal, China, and Tibet.

The narrative also includes a cautionary true story: a Christian loaned $3,000 to a man in trouble who promised to repay but never did. Three weeks later, the man and his girlfriend died, falling into a Christless grave. The friend had forgotten to pray for the man’s protection from judgment. Jesus teaches that believers have the solemn responsibility to pray for those who use them spitefully (Matthew 18:6).

One who ceases praying because of unanswered prayers might have misunderstood God's conditions. Scripture says that "we receive from Him whatever we ask, provided we keep His commandments and do what pleases Him" (1 John 3:22). God is always watching to see if our lives please Him.

Believers are encouraged to pray that the Lord reveal any obstacles hindering their prayer life to become effective in prayer. Jesus promised that if people "ask, seek, and knock," they will receive, find, and have doors opened to them (Matthew 7:7).

This story of prayer, drawn from Scripture and history, is a call to faithful, persistent, and sincere communication with God, recognizing His power to answer and the need for a purified, Spirit-guided heart.

Title: Secret, The
Subject: Basic Gospel
Author: Chick
Responses:
Once there was a man named Roy Davis who was caught in a cycle of violence and despair. One night, police officers mistakenly came to his house, asking if they could see his wife. Roy, who was drunk and fearful, told them she was sleeping and didn't want to wake her. But when the police insisted, they found her bruised and beaten. Roy’s own son shouted at him, declaring he hated him for hurting his mother. The wife explained her injuries as an accident, but the pain in the family was clear.

The son, Jason, vowed that when he grew up, he would kill Roy for hurting his mother. Despite this, the mother comforted Jason, apologizing for the nightmare he had to endure and pleading for help as she looked to the future with fear. The family was broken, caught in a dangerous and painful mess.

Two days later, Roy met Pastor Hunt, who offered him a free Bible and a chance to talk. Roy shared his painful secret: he was a drunk and a wife-beater, feeling hopeless and at the end of his rope. Despite trying, Roy couldn't change his destructive ways.

Pastor Hunt explained that the reason Roy couldn't change was because he was spiritually dead due to sin—a condition every person shares because of the original sin of Adam and Eve. But the pastor also shared hope: God loves us so much that He sent His Son, Jesus Christ, to die on the cross to save us. Jesus’s death was not for His own sins—since He never sinned—but for all of ours. Three days later, through God's power, Jesus rose from the dead, defeating sin and death forever.

The pastor urged Roy to repent and accept Jesus Christ to be born spiritually anew, with all sins forgiven and a new life begun. Roy expressed a desperate desire to change, promising to try with the preacher's help, and asked Jesus to come into his heart.

Almost immediately, Roy felt different — he knew God had set him free. He wanted to share the good news with his wife and son and began working on making amends. Pastor Hunt advised Roy to ask his family’s forgiveness and to show through his actions that God had truly changed him. Roy was confident that God would heal his home.

A week later, Roy surprised his wife with flowers instead of anger, promising that liquor would never again be in their home and that he would never hurt them again. He credited God's strength for his transformation. Overcome with remorse, Roy apologized to his family for everything he'd done and asked for their forgiveness.

Two months later, Jason expressed his love for his father and a desire to accept Jesus and be like him. The family thanked the Lord for saving their whole household.

28 years later, Roy died suddenly of a heart attack but entered glory, greeted as a faithful servant by God. At Roy's funeral, his wife told others how blessed she was to have had such a loving husband, now perfect in heaven.

The story concludes with a message to readers: God knows every secret, and just as Roy couldn't change on his own, neither can you; only God can bring true change. The invitation is open to receive Him today.

Title: Set Free
Subject: Basic Gospel
Author: Chick
Responses:
Once, all people were bound by the chains of sin, following the devil into a dark and fiery fate, as the Bible speaks in Romans 3:23, reminding us that "For all have sinned, and come short of the glory of God." The path they trod seemed right to themselves, but Proverbs 14:12 warns, "There is a way which seemeth right unto a man, but the end thereof are the ways of death."

From the very beginning, sin was set into human nature. Psalm 51:5 declares, "Behold, I was shapen in iniquity; and in sin did my mother conceive me." This original sin ensured that death would pass upon all men, for all have sinned, as Romans 5:12 explains.

Like unclean things swept away by the wind, humanity was captive to this sinfulness, Isaiah 64:6 tells us, "But we are all as an unclean thing... and our iniquities, like the wind, have taken us away." The devil cast many into the depths of darkness and eternal death, and the lamentation "Who shall deliver me from the body of this death?" from Romans 7:24b captures the desperate cry of mankind.

Yet, in His mercy, the Lord looked down from heaven upon mankind, seeking those who would understand and seek Him, as the Psalmist says in Psalm 14:2. God did not send His Son to condemn the world but to save it through Him, as John 3:17 reveals.

The devil tried to cling to the souls of men, but Jesus reached out to them, questioning in Mark 8:37, "What shall a man give in exchange for his soul?" Jesus, the Son of Man, came not to be served but to serve, giving His life as a ransom for many, according to Mark 10:45.

God's love for the world was infinite, so He gave His only begotten Son, that whoever believes in Him should not perish but have everlasting life, as John 3:16 unfolds. Jesus’ death on the cross was followed by three days in the heart of the earth, fulfilling Matthew 12:40's prophecy. Then came the resurrection, and the angel declared, "He is risen!" in Matthew 28:6.

Jesus, who lives forever, declared in Revelation 1:18 that He holds "the keys of hell and of death." When the bonds of sin were broken as Jesus freed the captive, the chains were cut by an angel, symbolizing liberation.

Romans 10:9 promises salvation to those who confess Jesus as Lord and believe in His resurrection. John 6:37b assures, "And him that cometh to me I will in no wise cast out."

Those who accept this gift are welcomed into heaven, receiving the praise, "Well done, thou good and faithful servant," as Matthew 25:21 celebrates.

But still, many remain chained, moving toward destruction, as Luke 19:10 reminds, for the Son of Man came to seek and save the lost. Yet Jesus reaches out to all, bidding them to believe in God and Himself, assuring peace and freedom, as John 14:1 and John 8:36 say.

The joy in heaven is great when a sinner repents, Luke 15:10 proclaims, "There is joy in the presence of the angels of God over one sinner that repenteth." And so, whoever calls upon the name of the Lord shall be saved, as Romans 10:13 concludes.

Thus, through Jesus Christ, weary souls can be freed from the bonds of sin and death, embraced in love, and welcomed into eternal life.

Title: Sin Busters
Subject: Ten Commandments
Author: Carter
Responses:
A man is forcefully arrested by police officers who accuse him of a crime, calling him a bigot. Nearby, two men discuss drug smuggling, with one revealing he got ten kilos from Colombia.

Students at a school talk about a boy who was punished for putting the Ten Commandments on the bulletin board. They debate why this is problematic, realizing it’s against the law to talk about the Bible or God in school anymore.

A teacher begins explaining the origin of the Ten Commandments, recounting how around 1500 B.C., God freed 3 million Hebrew slaves from Egypt using Moses as their leader. God performed many miracles to aid them, including drowning Pharaoh’s army, but despite these wonders, the Hebrews were rude and ungrateful. They complained about the lack of food and water after escaping Egypt, which frustrated Moses.

God provided "manna" from heaven to feed the Israelites, but they despised it. He also gave them water from a rock, another miracle, yet they still complained, causing God to keep them wandering the desert for 40 years. As former slaves, the Israelites had learned Egyptian evil ways, but because they descended from Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, God intended to teach them His ways.

God summoned Moses up Mount Sinai, where the mountain was ablaze and quaking in God’s presence. Alone and terrified, Moses witnessed God’s finger inscribing the Ten Commandments onto stone tablets. These tablets represented God’s holy law.

The First Commandment states that no other gods should be worshiped besides God. It forbids false gods like Buddha, Allah, and many others, including money, fame, and fortune, which God will not tolerate.

The Second Commandment strictly forbids making or bowing to any graven images or likenesses of anything in heaven, earth, or water. God commands that no one should bow to anything except Him.

Today, much of the world participates in idolatry, which God considers an abomination. The Third Commandment prohibits taking God’s name in vain. This is so serious that in Old Testament times it was punishable by death, a warning that applies even for those who swear using Christ’s name.

The Fourth Commandment instructs the children of Israel to keep the Sabbath day holy, resting one day a week to worship God.

The Fifth Commandment commands honoring one’s father and mother, emphasizing respect for parents, with a story illustrating tragic consequences when this is not followed.

The Sixth Commandment forbids murder, promising eternal punishment for murderers. A courtroom scene shows a murderer trying to escape justice, but God keeps records of all.

The Seventh Commandment forbids adultery, warning that sexual sin has serious consequences, including disease and spiritual death. A man tries to justify his affair, but the truth about its consequences is spoken.

The Eighth Commandment forbids stealing, the Ninth forbids lying against neighbors, and the Tenth forbids coveting what belongs to others. Despite these commandments, people hated the laws and continued sinning.

God kept the Israelites in the desert for 40 years until all the disbelieving adults died. Only Joshua and Caleb, who trusted God, entered the Promised Land. One sin prevented Moses from entering when he hit a rock to get water instead of speaking as God commanded.

The Israelites’ rebellion against the Ten Commandments caused their demise in the desert. The only person ever to keep all the commandments was Jesus Christ, who was perfect because He was God incarnate, born without sin.

Jesus gave His life for humanity’s sins because people couldn’t keep the commandments perfectly, showing the need for a Savior. Those who believe in Jesus will have eternal life and avoid hell.

The boy wonders why no one has told him about Christ and the Ten Commandments and questions why schools have banned this message, learning that a worldly system controls schools and opposes Christ.

He realizes that schemes hiding God’s laws won’t save him but understanding and following Jesus as his only hope will. The boy prays, asking Jesus to save him, acknowledging his need for salvation through calling on God’s name, quoting Romans 10:13.

Title: Sin City
Subject: Homosexuality
Author: Chick
Responses:
The story begins with a tense scene at a Gay Pride parade. Malcolm Wesley, holding a sign that reads “HOMOSEXUALITY IS AN ABOMINATION! SEE LEV. 20:13,” stands defiantly in opposition to the parade. The crowd shouts angrily at him, with some yelling to run him over, call him a gay basher, or even kill him. Police officers arrive and place Malcolm under arrest. They threaten to shoot the rest of the parade participants and order to kill footage that might expose their actions.

Two days later, Malcolm is formally charged with a hate crime for his actions opposing the parade. The officers emphasize that no one stops their parade and express violent intent towards Malcolm. However, the charges can be dropped if Malcolm changes his hateful attitude. To facilitate this, they bring in Reverend Ray, a Bible scholar and openly gay minister, alongside a man named Zanah, who declares his hatred for Malcolm's beliefs.

As the news spreads, Bob is informed that Malcolm is in the county hospital under arrest for a hate crime. Despite initial skepticism about the charges, Bob rushes to the hospital. The officers explain that the charges will be dropped if Malcolm listens to Reverend Ray, who will help him understand.

At the hospital, Reverend Ray tries to convince Malcolm that God loves all His children, including gays, and that people are born that way because God made them. Malcolm protests, mentioning the biblical story of Sodom and Gomorrah, but Reverend Ray counters that the real sin there was arrogance and inhospitality, not homosexuality. Malcolm initially struggles to understand but is guided through scripture. The hospital room brightens as Malcolm experiences a spiritual healing, and he gratefully acknowledges the change alongside Reverend Ray.

The narrative then shifts to the biblical account of Sodom and Gomorrah. God tells Abraham about His plans to destroy Sodom due to its wickedness. Abraham pleads for the city to be spared if even a few righteous people remain, but there are not ten righteous in all the cities of the plain. God sends angels to rescue Lot, Abraham’s nephew, but the men of Sodom attempt to sexually assault the angels. Consequently, God’s judgment strikes, and the cities are destroyed in flames, casting all inhabitants into hell.

The story emphasizes that homosexuality is a serious sin with biblical warnings and that God’s eyes see all actions, recording everything. Malcolm tried to warn others of God's coming judgment but almost faced death himself for it. He reflects on his past actions—holding rallies, cursing pastors, and preaching controversial messages—and fears he may be condemned.

The narrative stresses that all sin, including homosexuality, leads to hell unless one finds salvation through Jesus Christ. Malcolm is urged to repent and accept Jesus as his Savior, who sacrificed Himself to cleanse humanity’s sins. The story refutes the idea that Jesus was only a man, affirming He is God who rose from the dead.

Jesus’s own words are quoted, teaching that He is the only way to heaven. Malcolm wonders about other religions but concludes there is only one way—through Jesus. He repents sincerely, asking for forgiveness and salvation.

With faith, Malcolm experiences a transformation, feeling like a new person. He thanks God for revealing the truth to him. The story ends by addressing the reader, urging them to choose Jesus Christ to have their sins forgiven and receive eternal life. If they do nothing, they remain condemned. The final message is a call to "Choose Christ right now."

Title: Sissy?, The
Subject: Basic Gospel
Author: Carter
Responses:
The story begins with two truck drivers, Duke and Billy Joe, having a conversation while resting beside their rigs. Duke tells Billy Joe about a daring incident where he knocked a man through a plate glass window and into the street. Billy Joe admires Duke's toughness, but Duke clarifies that surviving in this world requires being tough because it's "a man's world."

As they prepare to get some food, Billy Joe points out a message on the back of a truck that bothers him. Duke dismisses it, calling Jesus a "sissy." Unexpectedly, a man overhears their conversation and challenges Duke's judgment of Jesus. The man, who owns the rig they're examining, invites the two to join him for supper, which they accept.

At the dinner table, Duke wonders how he ended up in this situation. The conversation shifts towards Jesus and what Duke thinks of him. Duke claims any man who turns the other cheek is a chump. The man counters with a thoughtful analogy: if God became a man with immense power, who would win a fight between God and a challenger?

Billy Joe interjects, suspicious of the fairness of such a fight. The man responds that Jesus, the "God-man," would win, but the fight wouldn't be fair since Jesus is also God. He explains that Jesus created the universe and was God in the flesh.

Duke and Billy Joe express confusion about the teachings, to which the man responds with a parable: if their house was on fire and someone didn't warn them, how would they react? Duke angrily says he would curse and never forgive the person.

The man warns Duke that his house is on fire—meaning his soul is in danger—and expresses concern for his eternal fate, saying Duke is blinded. He cites Bible verses indicating all have sinned and might be doomed to hell unless they change.

Duke angrily protests, but the man insists that God's judgment is real. Billy Joe voices confusion over the good things Duke said and what it means for him to not have to go to hell. The man offers clarity, explaining that Jesus was brutally beaten and crucified for sins, including Duke's.

He shares verses describing Jesus' suffering, death, and resurrection, explaining that Jesus' sacrifice provides a way to wash away sins. He tells Duke that when Jesus returns, he will defeat evil and bring justice.

The man describes the final judgment, urging Duke to repent and accept Jesus' forgiveness to avoid eternal punishment. Duke asks if he can pray for salvation, and the man welcomes him to join in prayer.

Later, a cook observes the men praying and wonders what's going on. The next day, Duke tells Billy Joe that through their prayer meeting, he discovered that Jesus had more guts than any man he ever knew, and he loves him for that. Billy Joe agrees wholeheartedly.

The story concludes with Duke and Billy Joe transformed, embracing faith and the courage it instills.

Title: Sky Lighter, The
Subject: Islam
Author: Chick
Responses:
A man solemnly informs a father that his daughter-in-law has died and that he could not save her. The father, concerned, inquires about the baby. The man reveals that the baby boy lives, describing him as healthy, beautiful, and strong. He vows to raise the child as his own son.

The man announces that the baby will be named Abdulla and promises that he will make them proud. He envisions their people cheering for Abdulla and calls him a future great warrior. He continues, telling Abdulla that at a significant moment, he will light up the sky, and in celebration, candy will be passed out, and his photo will be shown to neighbors dancing in his honor.

Four years later, as Abdulla grows, he is taught about the Qur’an and the concept of jihad. When asked what he thinks of that, Abdulla responds with enthusiasm, expressing praise for Allah. An elder explains that Abu-Bakr, the first caliph after Prophet Muhammad, declared that even if a person had one foot in Paradise, Allah would not allow him to enter if he did not fight in jihad.

In a classroom setting, children are taught that the only sure way to achieve Paradise in Islam is to sacrifice your life in jihad. Abdulla is told that he must slay the idolatrous non-Muslims wherever they are found, as prescribed in the Qur’an. They are promised a heavenly reward for this sacrifice.

Abdulla learns that his own father, Ahmed, tried to become a martyr by using a “heavenly robe” that failed to explode, leading to his imprisonment. His father was caught and beaten by enemies who stopped him. A teacher encourages Abdulla, saying this is why he was born and that Allah will bless him with special honors.

As Abdulla and other young boys are prepared, an instructor describes what will happen when their bombs explode, killing infidels around them. They are told they will be given a palace of pearls with 70 beautiful houses. Promises are made that 70 virgins, even more beautiful than imagined, await them, along with the strength and appetite of 100 men to enjoy eternity.

One day, Abdulla's childhood friend, Yusuf, suddenly appears, surprising Abdulla by revealing he had heard that Abdulla and his uncle were killed in an accident. Yusuf explains that it was only his uncle Salman who was badly hurt but survived. Abdulla invites Yusuf to a secluded place to tell him everything about the accident, away from prying ears.

Yusuf recounts seeing a truck crashing with bright lights, a loud noise, and then darkness. He was hospitalized with broken legs, and the doctor spent time telling him strange yet wonderful things. Yusuf explains they were talking about how Abdulla might want to kill himself to go to Paradise forever, but he discovered a way to heaven without blowing himself up.

Yusuf introduces Abdulla to the concept of the "People of the Book" and that his doctor gave him a Bible, which shocks Abdulla. Yusuf urges Abdulla to trust him and listen. Yusuf talks about prophets like Abraham, Moses, and especially Jesus, who came from God’s Father and said he is the Son of God.

They discuss how Jesus said, “I am,” and will come in the clouds of heaven, an overwhelming and amazing claim. Yusuf explains that Jesus came to save everyone because all are lost due to sin, and only God’s blood, through Jesus’ sacrifice, can wash away sins.

An elderly woman expresses concern over Abdulla, who was last seen slipping into a shed with Yusuf. Suspicious, people decide to check on them. Yusuf shares that he accepted Jesus as his Savior because Jesus said He is the way, truth, and life. Yusuf warns Abdulla that Satan and mullahs want him dead and that only children are encouraged to die this way, never the old men.

The woman sneaks up to listen to Abdulla and Yusuf's conversation, warning Abdulla not to kill himself and not to listen to those who lie. Suddenly, Abdulla is caught between the pressure from his people to fulfill a martyrdom mission for Allah and his growing belief in Jesus’ teachings. Despite threats and anger from others, Abdulla struggles with his choice.

Twenty minutes later, Abdulla lights up the sky with an explosion, killing many, fulfilling the mission. As a result, Abdulla dies, a victim of the pressures and beliefs that shaped his life. The story closes with a warning that judgment follows after death, and a stark message from Jesus about the eternal fate of all, urging belief in Christ as the only way to salvation.

The narrative contrasts the promise of violence and martyrdom in jihad with the message of salvation through Jesus, urging readers to reflect deeply on their beliefs and choices.

Title: Slugger, The
Subject: Sports
Author: Chick
Responses:
In the thrilling Game Seven of the World Series, the Hurricanes were trailing 4 to 1 in the bottom of the ninth inning with two outs. The bases were loaded, and Frank Stone, famously known as The Slugger, stepped up to the plate. With a powerful swing, he hit the ball deep to center field, the crowd erupting in cheers as it disappeared over the fence, securing the Hurricanes' victory in the World Series.

But something was immediately wrong with The Slugger. The next day, his manager proudly announced they had signed a $150 million contract with The Slugger, who also mentioned a $50 million shoe deal. At his mansion, Frank boasted to his friend Oscar about his wealth, fame, power, and the limitless things he could have. Oscar, however, challenged him, saying Frank had nothing of true value. When Frank angrily asked what Oscar meant, Oscar explained that someday Frank would die, and none of his riches would matter. The only thing he truly needed—something money couldn't buy—was his soul.

Frank angrily dismissed Oscar, asserting he made more money in one year than Oscar ever would in his lifetime. He ordered Oscar to shut up and get back to work despite feeling pain in his shoulder. That night, while attending a lavish party, Frank enjoyed his prestige and the admiration of others, feeling superior to Oscar.

Determined, Frank decided to confront Oscar. But when The Slugger opened Oscar's door, he was shocked by what he saw. Meanwhile, Oscar earnestly prayed for Jesus to show Frank that he was lost and needed salvation. Yet Frank reacted with anger and told Oscar never to pray for him again.

Two weeks later, Frank visited the doctor about his shoulder pain. The news was grim. The doctor informed him that he had terminal cancer that had spread through his shoulder and chest, giving him only a few weeks to live. Frightened and desperate, Frank asked Oscar to see him in his study and admitted he was scared. He asked Oscar if he would pray for him.

Oscar promised honesty, explaining that Frank was headed for hell but didn't have to be. He recounted a real friend who told him he was a sinner on his way to hell and then shared the good news that God loved him so much He sent Jesus Christ to die for his sins. Oscar cited biblical promises of forgiveness, salvation, and eternal life through faith in Jesus Christ.

Frank listened as Oscar explained how he had repented and trusted Christ as his Savior, changing his life forever. Oscar encouraged Frank to accept Jesus, telling him there was no guarantee of tomorrow and that the time to trust Christ was now. Frank prayed, confessing his sins and placing his trust in Jesus. He felt a huge weight lift from his shoulders and was no longer afraid to die.

A few weeks later, Frank Stone passed away. At heaven’s gate, he was welcomed warmly, confirming his name was written in the Book of Life. Back at the mansion, friends gathered for the reading of Frank's will. The reading revealed that Frank had asked Oscar to explain to everyone how Christ had saved him and to receive Jesus as their Savior. Frank left his $145 million estate to Oscar, trusting him to use it wisely.

The story concluded with a heartfelt message from Frank, urging readers to trust Jesus Christ as their Savior, emphasizing that fame, money, and earthly possessions could never buy eternal life or peace. His greatest wish was for everyone to have a personal relationship with Jesus, the most valuable gift anyone could receive.

Title: Sneakers
Subject: Basic Gospel
Author: Carter
Responses:
Once upon a time, a father promised his young son Johnny that when he got rich, he would buy land for him. But Johnny only wished for one thing: a pair of sneakers to keep his feet warm. The father assured Johnny he would buy the sneakers as soon as he got paid, and Johnny trusted his daddy wholeheartedly.

Excited about this promise, Johnny told his mother that his daddy was going to buy him shoes. His mother praised Johnny’s father as a good man. But when the father was paid at work, some men nearby whispered that they should take the money away from him.

Instead of buying the shoes, the father was persuaded to stop by a bar for a drink. The men at the bar convinced him to gamble his money, promising he could double it. Unfortunately, John lost repeatedly, and the bartender kept serving him drinks until closing time.

When John returned home drunk, his wife asked where the money for food was. John, confused and angry, said he didn't know what happened to the money and needed sleep. When Johnny asked about his sneakers, his father, sick and aching from a headache, told Johnny to go away.

Johnny pleaded with his father, saying he trusted him, but John told Johnny to leave and shut up. Despite the painful rejection, Johnny expressed his love for his daddy and Jesus. His mother prayed to God to help her husband stop lying so he could go to heaven and to make him buy Johnny his shoes.

The next payday, John's friends tried to convince him to drink again. Despite his wife’s concern, he gave in to their pressure. That night, John was thrown out of the bar because he was drunk, while his wife worried about him.

John returned home drunk and disheveled. His wife scolded him for breaking his promise and urged him to find a job so they could eat. John insisted he was a proud man who earned his money and said Johnny’s place was at home, not begging on the street.

John promised before God that he would be a good husband and father, stop gambling, and bring home his salary to buy Johnny the sneakers he wanted. His wife and son hoped he would keep his word.

On payday, John promised he would come home with Johnny’s shoes and the money to provide for the family. Johnny was excited, and his mother warned him of an approaching storm.

When John received his pay, the boss warned him to hurry home because the storm was getting worse. John's friends invited him to the bar, but he declined, determined to get shoes for his son.

Despite the cold rain and howling storm, his friends convinced him to have one drink, promising they would pay for it. John's wife prayed desperately to God for John to resist the temptation.

Suddenly, lightning struck the bar, causing a great explosion, and the building burned down. John’s wife believed that the hand of God had saved her husband. She chose sneakers from the store, believing her son would love them.

But the storm destroyed the bridge over the river, blocking John’s way home. At 1 a.m., Johnny woke to the cold night, searching for his sneakers and begging his father to come back.

When his mother heard Johnny calling, she rushed out, crying for God’s help. Meanwhile, Johnny lay outside, hearing beautiful music and asking if Jesus was really his.

At 10 in the morning, John returned home crying. He brought Johnny’s sneakers but was devastated to learn that Johnny had died of pneumonia during the storm. The family mourned, and the pastor comforted John, explaining that he could see Johnny again in heaven.

John was overwhelmed with guilt and sobbed, asking God for forgiveness. He admitted he had gambled, lied, and been a drunkard, begging for mercy.

Finally, John prayed for Jesus to come into his heart and be his Savior, hoping to be reunited with Johnny in heaven. Filled with sorrow but newfound faith, John thanked the Lord Jesus for His grace.

And so, through trials and loss, John learned the importance of keeping promises, relying on faith, and embracing the love and forgiveness offered by God.

Title: Snowflake?
Subject: Basic Gospel
Author: Carter
Responses:
The story begins with a teacher announcing that for Dress-Up Day, students must dress as their favorite storybook characters. She points out to the class that, just like the unique six-sided snowflakes that fall to the ground as snow, each student is different and unique in their own way.

The teacher explains that while there are 35 basic types of snowflakes, no two are exactly alike — much like the students themselves. She asks what they have learned today, and one student responds proudly, "I'm unique—just like everyone else!" However, the teacher notes that there are other kinds of snowflakes.

Some snowflakes avoid responsibility by pretending to be what they are not. Others try to change the rules just for themselves, each claiming to be the biggest victim and demanding special treatment. The teacher explains that snowflakes even twist words, taking offense at being questioned about things like their gender or age.

A scene of protesting highlights the conflict over tolerance and free speech, with people accusing others of hate while demanding the right to say whatever they want, even if it contradicts the message of love they secretly oppose. Tensions rise as “free speech” is contested and misunderstood.

The story shifts to a more personal example of selfishness in relationships, where one partner says relationships should be about give and take, but the other says, “You give and I take!” This raises the question of whether snowflakes are really unique or simply selfish.

The narrative moves to a spiritual perspective explaining that selfishness started long ago in heaven with Lucifer, who arrogantly asked why he shouldn’t be worshipped, believing himself perfect. Lucifer, described as once perfect, stretched his wings over God's throne, seeking to exalt himself above God. His pride led to a fall.

Lucifer convinced a third of the heavenly host to join him in rebellion against God. They were defeated and cast out of heaven, becoming angry devils bearing the consequences of this insurrection. Lucifer, now known as Satan, focused his hatred on mankind, aiming his revenge at the first humans, Adam and Eve.

The serpent (Satan in disguise) tricked Eve into eating from the forbidden tree of knowledge by appealing to her selfish desire, promising she would become like God, knowing good and evil. Eve fell for this deception and ate the fruit, then gave it to Adam, who also ate despite knowing it was wrong.

As a result, Adam and Eve realized they were naked and ashamed, having done evil in God’s sight. When confronted by God, Adam blamed Eve, Eve blamed the serpent, and the serpent suffered the consequence of losing his legs. This disobedience brought sin and death into the world, affecting all humanity.

The world became filled with selfish, sinful people headed for divine judgment. They are compared to sheep blindly following a path to destruction, recognizing deep down they are sinners like everyone else.

However, the story introduces Jesus as the exception, who lived a perfect, unselfish life. Jesus, the Son of God and Creator of everything, came from heaven to Earth to help humanity. God sent His Son because humans couldn't make up for their sins themselves.

Jesus humbled Himself, taking the form of a servant and dying on the cross to pay the price for everyone's sins. His death and resurrection opened the way for forgiveness and eternal life for those who believe in Him.

Each person is still unique, but in a new way: by trusting Jesus and asking for forgiveness, they receive grace and a new relationship with God. The story invites readers to seek Jesus, admit their sins, and accept His forgiveness.

After receiving Jesus, people are given the Holy Spirit to help them show God's unselfish love to others. The story concludes with encouragement to love and serve one another, emphasizing that God's love is the cure for selfishness.

It reminds readers that while everyone is unique, all can enter heaven through faith in Jesus Christ. Finally, it offers a simple invitation to admit one's sins, believe in Jesus' sacrifice, and receive Him into the heart—providing a personal decision form to mark that moment.

Title: Some Like it Hot
Subject: Hell
Author: Chick
Responses:
In a dark and fiery underworld, Freddy finds himself startled to see his grandfather among the tormented souls. "Freddy?" his grandfather asks, while Freddy replies in shock, "Is that you, Grandpa?" The old man, startled, asks, "What in blazes are you doing down here?"

Perched on a rocky ledge, Freddy explains he thought heaven was a place only for sissies. Grandpa questions if Freddy had seen any other relatives in this hellish domain. Freddy replies that everyone is down here on one level or another—except one. Curious, Grandpa inquires, "Who, Gramps, who?"

A winged tormenter approaches, telling Freddy his father didn't make it to heaven, but Freddy protests that his father is dead. Grandpa suggests maybe it's because his father is still alive. The tormenter points out that Freddy's father was buried five years ago, and Freddy suddenly realizes why his father didn’t make it—because he had "gone nuts on that Bible thing." The tormenter agrees with an "Amen, brother!"

Freddy remembers how his father, Henry, used to argue heatedly about the nature of hell. When Freddy claimed it was hotter than hell, Henry would retort, "Hell's hotter!" Freddy recalls hating Henry for saying there was no such place, and repeatedly telling him so.

Suddenly, Freddy and Grandpa are ordered to be brought to "the Master’s" office immediately, with warnings that the Master is not happy. They are led past threatening creatures and warned, "Don't touch the animals!" A giant, sinister beast growls as they proceed past a sign warning all to "Enter at your own risk."

Once before the Master, a fearsome horned figure tells Freddy he hated Henry and vice versa, acknowledging Henry was a difficult man who made his life hell. The Master reveals a secret—he is very religious and controls every major religion in the world. This revelation comes with a grandiose declaration: "In fact, I alone control every major religion in the world!"

The Master explains that their realm is overrun with religious leaders and their followers, including popes and holy men like Buddha and Muhammad, all of whom ended up in hell because they trusted their "good works"—all except Henry.

He explains there is only one way to heaven, and Henry found it, which changed his life. Freddy and Grandpa confess they don't remember Henry telling them about it. The Master threatens to prove his point by putting it on the big screen, revealing why Henry slipped through his fingers.

The Master recounts his own origin—a beautiful angel named Lucifer who guarded the throne of God. But when God refused to share the throne with him, Lucifer was cast out and became the ruler of hell. His greatest enemy was Jesus, God's Son, who defeated Lucifer's offer of worldly worship.

Lucifer told how he framed Jesus, turned people against Him, and witnessed Jesus' execution. He thought he had won when Jesus died on the cross, but was astonished when Jesus rose three days later and defeated his plans.

Now Lucifer admits he must fool the world’s people with a false gospel to keep them from believing in Jesus and going to heaven. He admits he can't touch Henry anymore but will try to punish Freddy and Grandpa.

The Master reveals that Henry trusted Jesus as his Savior, not his own good deeds, and led thousands away from hell. Freddy and Grandpa laugh at the gospel message, but now, trapped in hell, they can’t laugh anymore.

The story ends with a final warning that you don’t have to go to hell. It invites readers to confess their sins and accept Jesus as Savior, quoting biblical promises of salvation for those who call upon the name of the Lord.

It’s a tale of redemption, spiritual warfare, and the power of faith to triumph over darkness.

Title: Somebody Angry?
Subject: Israel
Author: Chick
Responses:
Early one morning at Weather Central, a meteorologist anxiously reported alarming news: a massive storm was rapidly intensifying. Winds had reached 150 mph, and the surge was building, indicating the storm could escalate to a category five hurricane. Urgently, officials sounded alarms and began immediate evacuations, warning that the storm had the potential to devastate the entire southern coastline.

By mid-morning, they anticipated the hurricane’s landfall in six hours, targeting the Texas-Louisiana coastal regions. However, evacuation efforts faced significant challenges as most roads were jammed in chaotic conditions. People crowded the streets, honking and pushing their way toward safety, some expressing fear about their survival and questioning why such calamity was happening.
